research_text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. What `SSLContext` governs, and what event/value this finding refers to

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and is a factory for `SSLSocketFactory`, `SSLServerSocketFactory`, and `SSLEngine` objects. It is initialized with optional key managers, trust managers, and a secure-random source.  
Source: <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html> ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The reported text refers specifically to the second argument (`tm`) of:

```text
SSLContext.init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)
```

The JDK API defines that argument as the “sources of peer authentication trust decisions.” A `TrustManager` determines whether the peer’s presented authentication credentials are trusted; if they are not, the connection is terminated. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The detector’s statement is therefore a **provenance/property claim about the `TrustManager[]` passed to `init`**: it says analysis observed an application-defined manager class in that array and did not establish that it came from a `TrustManagerFactory`. It is not, by itself, documentation that a particular runtime handshake, certificate chain, hostname check, enabled-protocol set, or negotiated TLS version is unsafe.

In particular, `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` is a request for a protocol implementation; it does **not** alone establish the enabled or negotiated protocol version. Oracle’s JSSE guide states that an `SSLContext` implementation may support more than the requested protocol, and that enabled protocols are controlled on the resulting socket/server-socket/engine using `setEnabledProtocols`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

---

### 2. Officially documented correct/safe usage and documented remediation

#### Documented trust-manager choices

The official JSSE documentation expressly permits two sources for `TrustManager` objects:

1. A provider-generated manager obtained from `TrustManagerFactory`; or  
2. A concrete application implementation of the relevant trust-manager interface.

The JSSE guide states: “`TrustManager` objects are created either by a `TrustManagerFactory`, or by providing a concrete implementation of the interface.” It also states that, when a custom `X509TrustManager` is required, an application may either create/register its own `TrustManagerFactory` **or implement `X509TrustManager` directly**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

Thus, an application-defined trust-manager class is **API-permitted**. The official API documentation does not say that a custom manager is categorically invalid or that every custom manager must be replaced with a factory-produced manager.

#### Documented provider/factory-oriented approach

Where normal X.509/PKIX trust processing is intended, the documented factory mechanism is:

- obtain a `TrustManagerFactory`;
- initialize it with a `KeyStore` or provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters`;
- obtain its `TrustManager[]`; and
- pass those managers to `SSLContext.init`.

`TrustManagerFactory.init(KeyStore)` initializes the factory from certificate-authority and related trust material; the provider typically uses the `KeyStore` as the basis for trust decisions. `getTrustManagers()` then returns a trust manager for each type of trust material. The standard `PKIX` factory algorithm produces `X509ExtendedTrustManager` objects that validate certificate chains under PKIX rules. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

The JSSE reference guide includes this factory-derived flow in its examples: factory initialization followed by passing `tmf.getTrustManagers()` to `SSLContext.init`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

#### Documented default alternative

The `SSLContext.init` API also permits `tm == null`. In that case, installed security providers are searched for the highest-priority appropriate factory implementation. The JSSE guide describes this as obtaining an appropriate trust manager from `TrustManagerFactory`; a null `SecureRandom` similarly selects a default random implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

#### What is—and is not—an official “remediation”

For a case where the intended trust policy is standard provider-backed PKIX validation, the official sources support using a `TrustManagerFactory` and its returned managers, or allowing the provider-selected default by passing a null trust-manager array. This is a documented migration direction, not a claim that all custom managers are erroneous. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

For a genuinely non-default policy, the official JSSE guide permits implementing `X509TrustManager` directly or creating/registering a custom `TrustManagerFactory`. Its illustrative custom-manager design delegates ordinary validation to a PKIX trust manager and applies alternative logic only if that default manager does not trust the credentials. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

**Important limitation:** the cited API and JSSE documents do not prescribe a universal code change for the detector message, and the CrySL source does not define what evidence is sufficient to establish `generatedTrustManagers[tm]`. Therefore, the official sources do not establish that replacing an application-defined manager with a factory result preserves the application’s intended trust policy.

Nothing in the reported condition establishes hostname-verification behavior. That must be evaluated separately under the application’s HTTPS/client endpoint-identification configuration; it should not be weakened as part of a trust-manager change.

---

### 3. Compatibility and migration documentation

#### Persisted formats

The `SSLContext` and `TrustManagerFactory` API specifications cited above do **not** define a persisted `SSLContext` format, serialized trust-manager format, or migration procedure for replacing a concrete `TrustManager` with factory-produced managers.

The documented persistent/configuration input relevant to factory trust management is trust material through a `KeyStore` or provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters`. The `TrustManagerFactory` API does not mandate a particular keystore format in the cited material. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

#### Wire formats

The cited sources do **not** say that changing from a custom trust manager to a factory-generated trust manager changes a TLS wire format. `TrustManager` governs peer-authentication trust decisions; the TLS protocol implementation and enabled-protocol configuration are separate concerns. This is consistent with the JSSE guide’s distinction between the `SSLContext` protocol request and the enabled-protocol list on created sockets or engines. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

However, compatibility can still change at the **authentication-policy** level if the trust anchors, provider, validation rules, or application-specific exceptions differ. The sources do not provide a general compatibility guarantee for such a change.

#### Platform-version support

`SSLContext` and `TrustManagerFactory` both exist since Java 1.4. The current Java SE 26 `SSLContext` API says every Java-platform implementation must support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`; it directs users to release documentation for other supported protocols. The current `TrustManagerFactory` API requires support for `PKIX`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification also cautions, by description, that a requested `SSLContext` name such as `TLS`, `TLSv1.2`, or `TLSv1.3` may support other SSL/TLS versions. Protocol enablement and actual negotiation must therefore be checked/configured separately rather than inferred from the `getInstance` literal. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))

#### Documented migration path

No formal migration path, versioned conversion procedure, or compatibility matrix is documented for this particular change. The closest documented alternatives are:

- configure `TrustManagerFactory` with the intended trust material and use its `getTrustManagers()` result;
- pass `null` for `tm` to select the installed provider’s highest-priority appropriate factory; or
- where custom behavior is actually required, directly implement `X509TrustManager` or provide a custom `TrustManagerFactory`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

**Source limitation:** these documents do not state which option preserves any particular application-specific trust exception, certificate pinning policy, private PKI policy, or hostname-validation behavior.

---

### 4. Exact CrySL rule matching and condition

Source requested:  
<https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl> ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Governing receiver type

The rule begins:

> `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`

So the rule is scoped to `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Verbatim matching/event clauses

The rule’s event clause is:

```text
EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;

	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);
	Engine := se1 | se2;
```

The forbidden clause is:

```text
FORBIDDEN
	getDefault() => Get;
```

The source declares these objects:

```text
java.lang.String protocol;
javax.net.ssl.KeyManager[] km;
javax.net.ssl.TrustManager[] tm;
javax.net.ssl.SSLEngine eng;
java.security.SecureRandom random;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Methods and parameter lists matched by the rule

Within the `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` specification, the source declares:

| Event | Method form declared | Parameter-list constraint in the CrySL source |
|---|---|---|
| `Get` | `getInstance(protocol)` | One argument bound to `protocol`, declared as `java.lang.String`. |
| `Get` | `getInstance(protocol, _)` | Two arguments; first bound to `protocol`; second is unconstrained (`_`). |
| `Init` | `init(km, tm, random)` | Three arguments bound to declared `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]`, and `SecureRandom` objects. |
| `Engine` | `eng = createSSLEngine()` | No arguments; return bound to declared `SSLEngine eng`. |
| `Engine` | `eng = createSSLEngine(_,_)` | Two arguments, both unconstrained; return bound to `eng`. |
| Forbidden | `getDefault()` | No arguments; mapped to `Get` by `=> Get` and independently forbidden. |

The declared order is:

```text
ORDER
	Get, Init, Engine?
```

Thus the rule requires `Get`, then `Init`, followed optionally by `Engine`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Conditions evaluated after matching

The source declares this protocol constraint:

```text
CONSTRAINTS
	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};
```

It also declares these requirements:

```text
REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];
```

And it declares these postconditions:

```text
ENSURES
	generatedSSLContext[this] after Init;
	generatedSSLEngine[eng] after Engine;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Accordingly, the supplied detector message corresponds most directly to the rule’s `generatedTrustManagers[tm]` requirement on the `tm` argument of the matched `init(km, tm, random)` event. The raw CrySL file does **not** define the implementation or evidentiary semantics of `generatedTrustManagers`; it only declares that predicate as a requirement. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Can it match a method that merely shares an API method name?

**No, not according to the rule’s declared scope.** The source specifies `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`; it does not declare an unrestricted, package-independent pattern for any method named `init`, `getInstance`, `createSSLEngine`, or `getDefault`. The raw source itself provides no additional dispatch-resolution semantics beyond that type scope, so implementation-specific details of how a detector resolves inheritance, overloads, or static calls remain unresolved from this source alone. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))
